strengths: Significance: Explicitly modeling asymmetric noise is a useful direction for bivariate causal discovery. SKEWD extends Gaussian location-scale models while retaining Gaussian noise as a special case.

Empirical evidence: Table 4 reports perfect SKEWD-LL accuracy across all six new skewed-noise benchmarks, including generalized-normal noise outside the fitted family. SKEWD-IT also improves substantially over LOCI-IT on the new heteroscedastic datasets. The ECM ablation in Table 2 provides useful evidence that refinement materially affects performance.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a practical synthesis of skew-normal regression, penalized location/scale splines, and causal-direction scoring. Although the ingredients and identifiability results are established, their combination addresses a meaningful modeling gap.

Presentation and transparency: The manuscript is generally well organized, reports individual benchmark results, and provides substantial optimization details in Appendix B. It explicitly acknowledges restrictions involving heavy tails, Gaussian marginals, and bivariate inference. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—likelihood scoring: Section 4 assumes both marginals are Gaussian, but the synthetic generator guarantees Gaussianity only for the cause; nonlinear mechanisms and skewed noise generally produce a non-Gaussian effect. Appendix A's Proposition 1 concerns standardizing already Gaussian variables and cannot establish Gaussianity of the effect. Gaussian working marginal scores do cancel after standardization, but this does not establish that the resulting conditional-likelihood comparison is a correctly specified joint-likelihood comparison. The paper needs to distinguish this heuristic from justified likelihood-based identification and evaluate alternatives that estimate the marginals.

Soundness—explanation of Gaussian-model failure: The motivating claim that skewness itself induces dependent residuals under Gaussian fitting is insufficiently qualified. For finite-variance LSNM noise, population Gaussian conditional-likelihood fitting with sufficiently flexible functions recovers the conditional mean f(X)+g(X)E[N] and standard deviation g(X)sd(N). The resulting standardized residual is independent of X even when N is skewed. Figure 1 therefore demonstrates a particular estimation failure, not an unavoidable consequence of symmetric likelihoods. A matched ablation fixing lambda=0 while retaining SKEWD's spline architecture, regularization, and optimization is needed to isolate the benefit of explicitly modeling skewness.

Soundness—ECM guarantee: In Section 3, the displayed updates for both psi and lambda use the previous iteration's parameters. In particular, the lambda update uses psi^(k), although psi^(k+1) has just been computed. These are not the sequential conditional maximizations described in the text, so the standard ECM ascent guarantee does not directly apply. The stochastic CMA-ES scale update also lacks an explicit acceptance safeguard ensuring that Q increases. The manuscript should correct or justify the updates and verify monotonicity; the current equations do not support the claimed optimization guarantee.

Evaluation and significance: The new benchmarks use only Gaussian causes, sigmoid mechanisms, and one sample size, and IGCI-G makes only one error across them despite its acknowledged model mismatch. This raises an unresolved possibility that benchmark regularities make direction identification unusually easy. Varying cause distributions, mechanism families, sample sizes, and noise families would better substantiate skewness robustness. General benchmark results are competitive rather than dominant: Table 1 gives SKEWD-IT 85.02% mean accuracy versus ROCHE's 87.69%, while Table 6 gives Tübingen accuracies of 66.57% for SKEWD-IT and 45.97% for SKEWD-LL, versus 77.27% for ROCHE.

Reproducibility and computational practicality: Appendix B specifies many useful hyperparameters, but the nested procedure includes 60 penalty candidates, eight-fold validation, multiple CMA-ES starts, and up to 5000 ECM iterations with further CMA-ES optimization. No wall-clock comparisons or scaling results quantify this potentially substantial cost. Repeated-run variability is also missing; standard deviations across heterogeneous datasets do not measure uncertainty from stochastic fitting. The code-availability footnote contains no usable repository address in the supplied manuscript.

Scope of support: The limitations discussion is welcome, but acknowledging Gaussian marginals and restricted noise families does not resolve their impact on the central reliability claims. Existing LSNM identifiability results concern the underlying distributional model; they do not establish consistency of the proposed penalized finite-spline estimator or its misspecified likelihood score. The empirical promise is clear, but the scoring justification, optimizer specification, and attribution of gains require substantive revision before acceptance.

strengths: Significance and originality: Explicitly modeling asymmetric noise in location-scale causal discovery is a useful extension. Combining skew-normal noise, penalized location/scale splines, and an adapted ECM procedure constitutes a discernible methodological contribution, although its components are established.

Empirical merits: The evaluation includes six new skew-noise settings and 13 established benchmarks. SKEWD-LL achieves perfect accuracy on the new datasets, including generalized-normal noise outside its assumed family. SKEWD-IT improves over LOCI-IT on all three new heteroscedastic settings (Table 4).

The ECM ablation is informative: refinement improves independence-based accuracy by approximately 28–34 percentage points on the new heteroscedastic datasets (Table 2), demonstrating that optimization materially affects the results.

Presentation and limitations: The overall exposition is organized, and Appendix B provides substantial optimization settings. The authors explicitly acknowledge restrictions concerning Gaussian marginals, heavy tails, and bivariate inference. No material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—likelihood scoring: Section 4 assumes both marginals are Gaussian, whereas the synthetic construction guarantees Gaussianity only for the cause; nonlinear mechanisms with skewed noise generally produce non-Gaussian effects. Appendix A's Proposition 1 applies to already Gaussian observations: standardization does not Gaussianize arbitrary variables. Gaussian marginal scores do cancel after standardization, but this algebra does not establish that the resulting score reliably identifies direction under marginal misspecification. The limitation is acknowledged, yet the strongest experimental claims depend on this unresolved issue.

Soundness—motivation and attribution: Skewness alone does not necessarily prevent Gaussian conditional fitting from recovering independent standardized residuals. With sufficiently flexible functions and finite noise variance, population Gaussian likelihood recovers conditional mean f(x)+g(x)E[N] and standard deviation g(x)SD[N], yielding residual (N−E[N])/SD[N], independent of X. Thus Figure 1 does not establish an inherent failure caused by skewness. A matched Gaussian version of SKEWD, retaining its splines, tuning, and optimization, is needed to distinguish noise-model benefits from estimation differences relative to neural-network LOCI.

Soundness—ECM specification: In Section 3, the update for lambda at iteration k+1 uses psi at iteration k, although psi has also been updated. These are not sequential conditional maximizations as written, so the claimed ECM monotonicity does not follow. The scale update additionally uses stochastic CMA-ES without a stated safeguard ensuring improvement of Q. The authors should correct or justify the updates and verify objective monotonicity; the scale/variance notation surrounding Equation 5 also needs correction.

Evaluation: The new benchmarks use Gaussian causes, sigmoidal mechanisms, and one sample size. IGCI-G makes only one error across these datasets, suggesting that their near-perfect results may reflect favorable distributional structure beyond skewness handling. Non-Gaussian causes, broader mechanisms, sample-size variation, and results separated by noise family would strengthen the robustness claim.

Significance of demonstrated gains: On established benchmarks, SKEWD-IT averages 85.02% accuracy versus 84.09% for LOCI-IT and 87.69% for ROCHE (Table 1). On Tübingen, it reaches 66.57%, compared with 77.27% for ROCHE and 81.59% for GRCI (Table 6). These results support specialized usefulness, but not broad superiority. Across-dataset standard deviations do not quantify uncertainty in paired improvements or stochastic optimization variability.

Reproducibility and practicality: The computationally extensive procedure uses 60 hyperparameter candidates, eight-fold validation, multiple CMA-ES fits, and ECM refinement, but provides no runtime comparison or convergence/failure statistics. The supplied manuscript's code-availability footnote contains no usable link. Spline knot placement, HSIC configuration, and whether residual testing uses independent held-out observations also remain insufficiently specified. Together with the soundness issues above, these gaps prevent a reliable acceptance recommendation.

strengths: Significance: Explicitly modeling asymmetric noise addresses a useful practical gap in bivariate location-scale causal discovery. The skew-normal family includes Gaussian noise, providing a coherent extension of existing models.

Originality: The contribution is a useful methodological adaptation: penalized splines for location and scale, skew-normal noise, and a combined CMA-ES/ECM estimation procedure. The paper appropriately attributes the underlying distribution, identification results, and earlier ECM methods.

Empirical merits: The evaluation includes multiple relevant baselines, 13 established benchmarks, and six new skewed-noise benchmarks. Table 4 reports substantial improvements over LOCI under strongly skewed heteroscedastic noise. Including generalized-normal noise tests some misspecification beyond the fitted family, and the ECM ablation provides useful evidence that refinement improves prediction.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript is generally well organized, with explicit objectives, algorithmic updates, and detailed result tables. Appendix B provides many optimization settings. The authors acknowledge the bivariate scope, heavy-tail limitations, and Gaussian marginal assumption; these disclosures are appropriate. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—likelihood scoring: Section 4 discards marginal likelihood terms by assuming Gaussian marginals for both variables. Although standardized Gaussian scores are equal, standardization does not make a non-Gaussian variable Gaussian; Appendix A's proposition explicitly requires Gaussian observations. The synthetic generator makes the cause Gaussian but generally produces a non-Gaussian effect. Thus, the strongest result—100% accuracy for SKEWD-LL—is obtained outside the stated justification for its joint-likelihood comparison. Experiments varying cause distributions and estimating marginal densities are needed to distinguish skewness robustness from favorable marginal-distribution asymmetry. IGCI-G's nearly perfect performance reinforces this concern.

Soundness—ECM updates: In Section 3, the displayed updates compute both the new location coefficients and the new shape parameter using the previous values of the other parameter. In particular, the shape update uses psi^(k), not the newly updated psi^(k+1). These are not sequential conditional maximizations, so the stated ECM monotonicity guarantee does not follow as written. The scale update also uses stochastic CMA-ES without describing an objective-improvement safeguard. The paper should correct or justify these updates and establish which procedure produced the reported results.

Soundness—explanation of Gaussian-estimator failure: Skewness alone does not force population residual dependence under Gaussian location-scale quasi-likelihood. With sufficiently flexible functions and finite noise variance, conditional mean and standard deviation yield standardized residuals equal to (N−E[N])/sd(N), which remain independent of the cause. The observed failures may therefore reflect function-class restrictions, regularization, or optimization. Since LOCI uses neural networks while SKEWD uses splines and a different optimization pipeline, a matched Gaussian ablation with lambda fixed to zero is necessary to attribute the gains specifically to skewness modeling.

Significance and evidential reach: The new benchmarks use Gaussian causes, sigmoidal mechanisms, and a single sample size. On established benchmarks, SKEWD-IT averages 85.02% accuracy versus ROCHE's 87.69%; on Tübingen it achieves 66.57% versus ROCHE's 77.27% and GRCI's 81.59%. These results support a specialized contribution, but not the broad robustness language. Repeated optimization runs, paired uncertainty estimates, and separate results for the pooled noise families would clarify reliability; standard deviations across different datasets do not quantify uncertainty in method comparisons.

Reproducibility and practicality: The code-availability footnote ends with 'publicly available under' but supplies no URL. Important details such as spline-knot placement and independence-test calibration are also not specified. The procedure involves 60 hyperparameter candidates, eight-fold validation, repeated CMA-ES fits, and ECM iterations containing further CMA-ES optimization, yet no runtime comparison or scaling analysis is reported. These omissions impede independent implementation and assessment of practical usefulness.

strengths: Significance: Handling asymmetric noise in heteroscedastic causal discovery is a useful problem. The skew-normal model offers a tractable extension of Gaussian LSNMs while retaining Gaussian noise as a special case.

Originality: The contribution is a practical synthesis of skew-normal regression, penalized additive splines, heuristic optimization, and ECM refinement for causal discovery. Extending existing heteroscedastic regression machinery to this setting is a meaningful methodological contribution.

Evaluation: The experiments cover 13 established bivariate benchmarks, additional skewed-noise datasets, and small multivariate graphs. Testing generalized-normal noise outside the fitted family's skewness and kurtosis ranges is particularly valuable. Table 3 also demonstrates substantial empirical benefits from refinement over the initial heuristic estimates.

Presentation and responsible reporting: The manuscript is generally well organized and supplies detailed equations, hyperparameters, and per-dataset results. It explicitly discusses marginal misspecification, computational limitations, and the risks of causal conclusions when assumptions such as causal sufficiency fail. No material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—ECM updates: Section 4 updates both psi and lambda using their previous values. In particular, the lambda update uses psi^(k), although psi^(k+1) has just been computed. These are simultaneous conditional updates, rather than the sequential maximizations required by the stated ECM argument; joint improvement of the Q-function is therefore not established. The scale update additionally uses stochastic CMA-ES without a stated ascent safeguard. The claimed likelihood monotonicity requires corrected updates or a separate justification. Equation (5) also inconsistently uses omega where the declared Gaussian notation requires omega squared.

Soundness—explanation of Gaussian residual failure: Skewness alone does not prevent Gaussian quasi-likelihood from recovering conditional means and variances. For a finite-variance LSNM, these are f(X)+g(X)E[N] and g(X)^2 Var(N), so correctly standardized residuals remain independent of X even when N is skewed. Figure 1 therefore demonstrates a particular estimation failure, not an intrinsic failure of Gaussian residual extraction. Comparing neural-network LOCI against a differently optimized spline model does not isolate the effect of the noise distribution. A matched lambda=0 ablation with the same representation, regularization, and optimization is needed.

Soundness—likelihood guarantees: Proposition 5.1 establishes only that common score contributions can be omitted; it does not establish consistency of the implemented score. Gaussian root models can be misspecified, including for the uniform roots used in Section 6.2, and general LSNM identifiability does not guarantee that this misspecified likelihood selects the true DAG. Appendix A.3's standardization argument applies to already Gaussian variables; standardization does not Gaussianize arbitrary marginals. The acknowledged limitation should also qualify the recovery claim in Section 5.2.

Evaluation and significance: The strongest result—perfect SKEWD-LL accuracy on the new benchmarks—uses exclusively Gaussian causes and a narrow sigmoidal mechanism family. IGCI-G makes only one error across these datasets, suggesting that favorable benchmark structure may explain substantial performance. Replacing Gaussian marginals with KDE reduces LSs accuracy to 79–84% (Table 11). On Tübingen, SKEWD-LL achieves 45.97% and SKEWD-IT 66.57%, versus 77.27% for ROCHE and 81.59% for GRCI. These results support a specialized benefit but do not establish broad reliability under skewness. Controlled variation of cause distributions, mechanisms, and sample sizes would strengthen the central claim.

Multivariate evidence: The experiment specifies SN(0,1,0.985), whose skewness is approximately 0.132, rather than 0.985. Unless this is a parameterization typo, it tests relatively mild asymmetry. Moreover, no PC-only reference or Gaussian conditional scorer using the same estimated MEC is reported, so the large advantage over methods with different graph-search procedures cannot be attributed specifically to skew-normal modeling.

Reproducibility and computational practicality: Appendix B gives useful implementation details but omits Bayesian-optimization budgets and search ranges, spline knot and centering conventions, and a clear account of whether independence testing uses held-out residuals. The concatenated multivariate spline bases also require identifiability constraints to justify the displayed matrix inverse. No measured runtimes accompany the nested cross-validation, multiple CMA-ES fits, and thousands of ECM iterations. Reported standard deviations across benchmarks do not quantify optimization variability or uncertainty in paired method comparisons. These omissions, together with the update inconsistencies, prevent reliable reproduction of the central method as written.

strengths: Significance: Addressing asymmetric noise in location-scale causal discovery is useful. The skew-normal model offers a tractable extension of Gaussian methods, and the experiments include GNO noise outside its supported skewness and kurtosis ranges.

Empirical merits: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy on all six proposed benchmarks. SKEWD-IT is competitive across established benchmarks, averaging 85.02% versus ROCHE’s 87.69% (Table 1). The ECM ablation also demonstrates substantial improvements over heuristic initialization, particularly for independence testing (Table 3).

Originality: The contribution is a practical integration of penalized skew-normal GAM estimation, evolutionary optimization, and causal scoring. Extending the existing heteroscedastic ECM approach to this setting is a discernible methodological contribution, although the underlying estimation and identifiability ideas are inherited.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is generally well organized, provides extensive supplementary results, and explicitly discusses marginal misspecification, computational limitations, and causal sufficiency. The impact statement appropriately warns against unsupported causal interventions; no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—optimization guarantee: The ECM updates as written do not establish the claimed likelihood monotonicity. On page 5, both the location-coefficient update and the shape update use the previous parameter values; specifically, the shape update uses the old location coefficients rather than the newly updated coefficients. These are simultaneous conditional updates, not the sequential conditional maximizations described in the text. Moreover, the scale update uses stochastic CMA-ES without a stated acceptance check ensuring that the Q-function increases. The algorithm needs correction or justification, together with evidence that the implementation follows a valid ascent procedure.

Soundness—attribution to skewness: Gaussian conditional maximum likelihood can recover the conditional mean and variance under non-Gaussian noise. For an LSNM with finite noise variance, standardizing by those population quantities produces an affine transformation of the independent noise. Thus, skewness alone does not imply dependent residuals under Gaussian fitting. The Figure 1 failure could reflect finite-sample estimation, regularization, or function-class differences. Comparing neural-network LOCI with spline-based SKEWD does not isolate these factors. A matched SKEWD ablation fixing the shape parameter to zero is needed to substantiate the central explanation.

Evaluation—benchmark confounding: All new bivariate benchmarks use Gaussian causes, directly matching SKEWD-LL’s marginal assumption. IGCI-G also makes only one error across these datasets despite its acknowledged misspecification. Furthermore, replacing Gaussian marginals with KDE reduces SKEWD-LL’s LSs accuracies from 100% to 79%, 82.5%, and 84% (Table 11). These findings suggest that favorable marginal structure materially contributes to the headline result. Controlled experiments varying cause distributions, noise variance, and skewness independently are needed before claiming broadly reliable discovery under skewed noise.

Soundness—identifiability versus scoring: Proposition 5.1 correctly removes likelihood terms shared across candidate DAGs, but it does not establish consistency of the proposed score. General LSNM identifiability does not ensure correct orientation with misspecified Gaussian root densities, restricted GAM conditionals, and heuristic optimization. Section 5.2’s recovery discussion needs explicit assumptions covering the complete fitted joint model. Appendix A.3’s cancellation is valid for Gaussian fitted scores; standardization itself does not make non-Gaussian observations Gaussian.

Significance and evaluation scope: The strongest performance is concentrated in the proposed synthetic setting. On Tübingen, SKEWD-LL achieves 45.97% and SKEWD-IT 66.57%, versus 77.27% for ROCHE and 81.59% for GRCI (Table 7). Multivariate experiments cover only sparse six- and ten-node graphs, without a matched Gaussian scoring method using the same PC-estimated MEC. Consequently, the large multivariate gains do not isolate the benefit of skewness modeling. The reported standard deviations across benchmarks also do not quantify uncertainty from sampling or stochastic optimization.

Reproducibility and technical presentation: Appendix B supplies useful implementation details, but omits important Bayesian-optimization settings, including search ranges and evaluation budgets, and provides no measured runtimes for the expensive nested optimization. Section 6.2 specifies noise as SN(0,1,0.985), where 0.985 denotes shape under Definition 3.3, whereas the bivariate skewness level 0.985 corresponds to shape 20. This ambiguity materially affects reproduction and interpretation of the multivariate experiment. These unresolved methodological and evidential issues outweigh the paper’s practical merits.

strengths: Significance: Noise asymmetry is a useful and practically motivated direction for location-scale causal discovery. Modeling skewness explicitly addresses a limitation of commonly used Gaussian and Student-t likelihoods.

Originality: The combination of skew-normal GAMs, penalized estimation, and causal scoring is a useful methodological extension. The contribution is primarily this integration and its empirical investigation, rather than a new identifiability result.

Empirical merits: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy on all six proposed skew-noise benchmarks, including GNO noise outside the assumed family. The ECM ablation reports substantial improvements, especially for independence testing. Evaluating 13 established benchmarks and including KDE marginal estimation provides valuable additional evidence.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is generally well organized and explicitly discusses marginal misspecification, computational limitations, and omitted interactions. The impact statement appropriately warns about confounding and harmful interventions from incorrect causal conclusions.
weaknesses: Soundness—optimization: The displayed ECM updates in Section 4 do not establish the claimed monotonic improvement. Both the location and shape updates use the previous iterate, although these parameters are coupled in the Q-function. This simultaneous update can decrease Q; a sequential conditional update should use the updated location when updating shape. The subsequent CMA-ES scale update also needs an explicit improvement safeguard. Because ECM refinement is a central contribution, the equations, implementation, and ascent claims need to be reconciled.

Soundness—multivariate parameterization: Appendix A.2 concatenates complete B-spline bases without stating centering or identifiability constraints. Each basis spans a constant, and second-difference penalties leave constants unpenalized. With multiple parents, shifting a constant between components therefore leaves both the fitted function and penalty unchanged, making the matrix inverted in the displayed location update singular. The actual constraints or numerical treatment need to be specified.

Soundness—attribution to skewness: Skewed noise does not inherently prevent Gaussian quasi-likelihood from recovering independent standardized residuals. With sufficiently flexible functions and finite noise variance, it targets E[Y|X]=f(X)+g(X)E[N] and Var(Y|X)=g(X)^2 Var(N), whose standardized residual remains independent of X. Figure 1 therefore demonstrates an estimation failure, but does not isolate skewness as its cause. A matched Gaussian version using the same splines, regularization, and optimization is needed to distinguish the benefit of skew-normal modeling from estimator differences.

Evidence and significance: The strongest results use Gaussian causes and a narrow family of sigmoidal mechanisms. Gaussian marginal scoring can itself favor the true direction in this design; IGCI-G also makes only one error across these datasets. Table 11 shows that replacing Gaussian marginals with KDE reduces SKEWD-LL's LSNM accuracy from 100% to 79–84%. This does not invalidate the Gaussian-source setting, but broader source distributions and controlled ablations are needed to support the general robustness claim. On Tübingen, SKEWD-IT achieves 66.57%, versus 77.27% for ROCHE and 81.59% for GRCI.

Theoretical scope: Proposition 5.1 correctly removes graph-invariant score terms, but does not prove that the implemented score selects the true graph. Generic LSNM identifiability alone does not establish consistency under Gaussian marginal misspecification, restricted GAMs, regularization, and heuristic optimization. The recovery statement in Section 5.2 should explicitly require correct specification of the relevant joint distributions and consistent estimation.

Reproducibility and evaluation: Appendix B provides useful settings but omits important Bayesian-optimization details, such as search ranges and evaluation budgets, and reports no wall-clock comparisons despite the nested optimization. The reported standard deviations across benchmarks do not quantify stochastic optimization uncertainty. The multivariate experiment also specifies SN(0,1,0.985), where 0.985 is the shape parameter rather than the high skewness coefficient used elsewhere; this needs clarification. These unresolved technical and evidential issues outweigh the promising empirical contribution.
